title: One Household's Plan Isn't a Community Plan

body.en: Your household has its own emergency plan sorted. Your neighbour, an elderly man living alone, does not — and during the last flood, nobody checked on him until a full day later. What's the right next step for your street?

choices.label: Organise a simple street-level plan: who checks on whom, and a shared meeting point
choices.consequence: Exactly this. Individual household plans leave gaps for people who live alone or can't prepare on their own — a community-level plan is what catches those gaps before someone goes a full day unchecked.

choices.label: Trust that someone else on the street will think to check on him
choices.consequence: This is precisely how he went unchecked for a full day — an assumption with no one actually responsible isn't a plan.

choices.label: Decide it's not your street's responsibility, just his family's
choices.consequence: In an emergency, distant family often can't reach someone in time — the people actually nearby are the real safety net, whether it's formally 'their responsibility' or not.
